lesson.title: Nagle's Algorithm and the Cost of Sending One Byte at a Time
lesson.summary: Nagle's algorithm batches small outgoing writes into fuller segments to avoid flooding the network with tiny, header-heavy packets, though it can interact badly with delayed acknowledgments in interactive applications.
lesson.body:
TCP lets an application write data in whatever chunks it wants, but the network does not treat all chunk sizes equally well. Consider an old-style interactive terminal session, where every keystroke the user types is handed to TCP as a separate one-byte write. Each of those bytes, if sent immediately, becomes its own TCP segment wrapped in an IP header and, further down, a link-layer frame, typically around 40 bytes of overhead to carry a single byte of actual data. On a network shared by many connections, a flood of such tiny segments wastes a large fraction of the link's capacity on overhead rather than payload, a pattern known as the small packet problem.

John Nagle's algorithm addresses this by making TCP more patient about when it sends small amounts of data. The rule is: if there is already unacknowledged data in flight for this connection, and the application hands TCP a new, small amount of data (smaller than one full maximum segment size), do not send it immediately. Instead, buffer it, and wait until either enough data accumulates to fill a full segment, or an ACK arrives for the data that is currently outstanding. Once that ACK arrives, whatever has accumulated in the buffer is sent as a single segment. If there is no unacknowledged data outstanding at all, meaning the connection is otherwise idle, small writes are sent immediately without delay, since there is no earlier data to wait on. The effect is that a burst of small writes from an application gets coalesced into far fewer, fuller segments, without ever holding data back when the connection has nothing else in flight to wait for.

This interacts in an important and sometimes troublesome way with delayed acknowledgments, a receiver-side optimization where TCP holds off sending an ACK for a short interval, often up to around 200 milliseconds, hoping to either piggyback the ACK on outgoing data of its own or coalesce it with the ACK for a subsequent segment, reducing the total number of pure ACK packets sent. Nagle's algorithm on the sending side is waiting for an ACK before it will send more small data; delayed ACK on the receiving side is waiting before it sends that ACK at all. In a request-response style interactive exchange, where each side is both sending small amounts of data and expecting to acknowledge the other's small amounts of data, these two optimizations can end up waiting on each other: the sender withholds its next small write until an ACK arrives, while the receiver withholds that ACK hoping to bundle it with data of its own that never comes quickly enough, so the ACK sits queued for the full delayed-ACK interval before finally being released. The net effect is a visible, repeating delay, often in the range of tens to a couple hundred milliseconds per exchange, that shows up as exactly the kind of inconsistent, bursty latency the concept of jitter describes, particularly damaging for applications like real-time gaming, financial trading, or remote terminal sessions where responsiveness matters more than bandwidth efficiency.

Because of this, applications sensitive to latency commonly disable Nagle's algorithm on their sockets using the TCP_NODELAY option, choosing to send small writes immediately rather than risk this interaction with delayed ACKs. This is a reasonable tradeoff for interactive or real-time traffic, where a few extra small packets on the wire matter far less than shaving tens of milliseconds off round trip latency, but it is the wrong choice for bulk, throughput-oriented transfers, where Nagle's batching genuinely reduces overhead without harming user-perceived responsiveness. The algorithm is not wrong, it is simply tuned for a different goal than some applications actually have, which is why TCP exposes the choice rather than making it unconditionally.
